query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying HfMoTaTiZr with a small amount of a low-density, ductile element such as Al can reduce the density of the alloy without sacrificing its strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g cm−3 and yield strength of 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of Al to the HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperature (up to 1000 °C) under compressive loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The addition of Al is expected to reduce the density of the alloy by replacing some of the heavier elements, while its ductile nature may help to improve the fracture toughness of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The reduction in density is expected to occur through the replacement of heavier elements with Al, while the improvement in fracture toughness is expected to occur through the introduction of a ductile element that can help to absorb energy and reduce the propagation of cracks.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in density of at least 5% without a significant sacrifice in yield strength at room temperature and elevated temperature.
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g cm−3 and yield strength of 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: The alloy's performance will be evaluated at room temperature and elevated temperature (up to 1000 °C) under compressive loading.
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Al to be added and the resulting microstructure and properties of the alloy are uncertain and require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Compressive testing of the Al-alloyed HfMoTaTiZr alloy at room temperature and elevated temperature.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the density of the Al-alloyed HfMoTaTiZr alloy is not reduced by at least 5% or the yield strength at room temperature and elevated temperature is significantly sacrificed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. Xu et al. [] reduced the density of the Ti50-xAlxV20Nb20Mo10 RHEA from 6.102 g/cm3 (Ti40Al10V20Nb20Mo10) to 5.876 g/cm3 (Ti30Al20V20Nb20Mo10) by adjusting the Al content, and the room-temperature specific yield strength increased from 147.49 MPa*cm3/g to 202.01 MPa*cm3/g. Although the density and specific strength of these alloys are significantly improved after the addition of aluminum, their plasticity is generally reduced. Therefore, choosing a refractory high-entropy alloy with both high strength and high plasticity as a matrix, and then reducing its density by adding light elements such as Al, is an effective method to obtain structural materials with high strength, low density, and good plasticity. The recently reported TaNbVTi alloy meets the requirements of the matrix very well []. Furthermore, Yang et al. [] reported that the arc-melted NbTiVTaAl0.25 HEA has a low density of 8.78 g/cm3 and reasonable plasticity greater than 50%. Nevertheless, the yield strength of this alloy is only 1330 MPa (specific strength of 151.48 MPa*cm3/g), which has the possibility of further improvement compared with most refractory high-entropy alloys.
